speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday, February 16, consideration in committee of the following proposed resolution-Mr. Dunning -Mr. Sanderson in the chair:
That the governor in council be authorized to raise by way of loan under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, an amount not to exceed in the whole the sum of seven hundred and fifty million dollars for paying or redeeming the whole or any portion of loans or obligations of Canada, and also for purchasing and withdrawing from circulation unmatured securities of Canada, and for public works and general purposes.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to oppose the resolution because I am opposed to the financial policy of this government, a policy which in my opinion is forcing the people of this country further and further into debt, resulting in increased taxation and a steady lowering of the standard of living of the people.
Some members appear to believe that the present system has operated satisfactorily in the past and that there is no reason why it cannot continue to operate satisfactorily in the future. But, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Lander-you) the other day, the present system is a debt-creating system, and so long as we operate under it our debts are bound to increase steadily until eventually our fixed debt charges may well be in excess of our total revenue.
What is the result of this system? In the field of physical accomplishment it is no doubt one of which we may well be proud. But in the economic field it is one which must be a matter of concern to every thinking individual. The record of the present system has been that of building up enormous unrepayable debts, federal, provincial, municipal and private, resulting in default on
Loan oj $750,000,000

bonds and mortgages, in bankruptcies and wholesale cancellation of debt, this very often taking place in the face of tremendous selfdenial and long hours of overtime on the part of the people. Perhaps the greatest condemnation of the present system is that it creates an artificial scarcity in the face of potential abundance, and restricts production in the face of actual want, thus causing starvation and destitution.
We find many people in their smug complacency telling us that the system has operated satisfactorily in the past. I would say that the present system is a dishonest one; because what moral right have we to mortgage the production of future generations? What right have we to place a debt against unborn generations? To my mind the present financial system is nothing more or less than a gigantic racket, wherein the Minister of Finance has been placed in the position of acting as a collector for these financial racketeers. We are told that this system is highly efficient and that it has operated satisfactorily, but I would say, satisfactorily from whose point of view? From that of the bankers, certainly. But a system which has operated so as to force the people of this country steadily further and further into debt can hardly be considered from their point of view a satisfactory system.
The motion is-
-to raise by way of loan under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, an amount not to exceed in the whole the sum of seven hundred and fifty million dollars for paying or redeeming the whole or any portion of loans or obligations of Canada, and also for purchasing and withdrawing from circulation unmatured securities of Canada, and for public works and general purposes.
WTe are opposed to the policy of the government as exemplified by this resolution, because we feel it is a policy which is largely responsible for the poverty that exists throughout the country; and it is our intention to move an amendment. I had hoped that this amendment would have been moved before I spoke, but it will be proposed, after I have finished, by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Landeryou).
We hear a great deal about the dangers of communism and fascism. The greatest protection against communism or fascism is a happy and contented people. Both these "isms" thrive on discontent, and discontent is rife from one end of this dominion to the other. The failure of this government to bring about any really progressive policy is responsible, more than any other single factor, for the growth of fascism and communism. For several years we have been told that the major problem is unemployment. The Bank [Mr. Quelch.l
of Canada report points out that unemployment must be regarded as a long-term problem. But 1 would point out that employment is merely a means to an end; that end is economic security for the people. The real problem therefore is not so much one of employment as of providing social security for the people.
Have we any reason to believe that this resolution will help to bring social security to the people? I am afraid that all we can expect is that it will help to bring about better conditions of a temporary nature, but eventually it must mean an increase of debt, resulting in more poverty. For generations the best brains of the world have been endeavouring to find ways and means by which the productivity of mankind could be increased, and to-day we have at last reached the position where we have actually created a surplus productive capacity both of manpower and of machine-power. We have emerged from an era of scarcity into one of abundance. We have now reached the stage where it is not only possible but logical that the people of this country should be able to enter an era of greater leisure. It is a picture of which we might well be proud. But what do we find? We find at the present time the Minister of Labour pitting his puny weight against the combined brains of the scientists. They on the one hand are making it possible for more and more people to be relieved of the heavy and long toils of labour; he on the other hand is trying to put more men back to work. Unquestionably he is fighting a losing battle, and I -would say it is a good thing that he is, because his policy is one of reaction.
What is the situation in Canada to-day? We have a great productive plant in the form of factories, farms and mines, working at only a small percentage of their capacity; great natural resources barely tapped; great reserves of energy, a large surplus of unused labour in the form of the unemployed; and, in addition, a favourable balance of payments in the neighbourhood of, I believe, $185,000,000. It is a glorious picture, and one of which we might well be proud. I suppose that if anybody who was unfamiliar with conditions in Canada were confronted with that picture he would immediately say, "Undoubtedly there cannot be any poverty in Canada; for you must be enjoying a very high standard of living". He would be justified in coming to that conclusion, because there can be no excuse for having a picture of that kind on the one side, and on the other approximately a million people on the verge of starvation, with thousands upon thousands suffering from a very low standard of living.

We hear hon. members and people outside the house criticize industry for not having more confidence, for not expanding; but how can industry expand when it is already in the unfortunate position of having difficulty in selling its products? It is true there is a large physical demand for goods in Canada to-day, but what good is that physical demand unless it is backed up by money? We therefore contend that steps will have to be taken to put money in the hands of the general consumer so that it will be possible to make that great physical demand effective against the production of the country. Until this is done it is useless to talk about industry expanding.
The reason for this 'condition-we have stressed it in this chamber many times, and I do not wish to labour the point-is that industry is not in a position to create, except in times of excessive capital goods construction, an effective demand for its own production. When, on March 14 of last year, I spoke in this chamber, I dwelt at some length on this subject, and I do not intend at this time to go over that field, but in passing I would merely mention what I believe are three of the main causes: (1) the practice of charging profits into prices without distributing purchasing power to pay those charges; (2) the practice of saving and the reinvestment of savings, which increases production without bringing about a corresponding increase in the effective demand of the people; and (3) the repayment of old debts, which results in a certain charge being put into prices to recover those debts, without a corresponding issue of purchasing power to pay them. As these deficiencies are occurring concurrently with production, and as production goes on continuously, it is quite obvious that a deficiency must occur continuously as well unless, as already stated, there is a certain definite volume of capital goods construction. I call that point to the attention of the Minister of Finance because when he spoke last year he said that we had absolutely ignored the question of capital goods construction; and yet when most of us have spoken on this point we have mentioned that there must be a certain definite volume of capital goods construction, or in other words you must maintain a definite relationship between capital goods construction and the production of consumption goods.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: What relationship?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
The very first time I spoke in this house at the first session I laid down the premise that industry could not create an effective demand for its own production unless you had a sufficient volume of capital goods
construction, so that the salaries, wages and dividends paid in that production were equal to the deficiency of purchasing power that existed as between total prices of consumer goods and the purchasing power distributed in their production. You have to maintain that relationship; otherwise there will be a lag in the demand for consumer goods. It must be obvious that there is a definite limit to the amount of capital goods production, that can be carried on because there is no use in building factories if you cannot sell the goods produced by the factories already in existence.
This resolution proposes the borrowing of money for capital goods. That is a very fine thing and in that way the deficiency might be made up temporarily. But, I repeat, inasmuch as the deficiency occurs continuously with production it stands to reason that you cannot make it up by borrowing money on a permanent basis. That money will have to be issued debt free if you are ever to make up the continuously recurring deficiency. It must be obvious that borrowing money to make up a continuously recurring deficiency can only result in steadily increasing debt. If, as we have done in the past, we can have the banks create money for our use, without that action resulting in inflation, then I say that there is no reason under the sun why under similar circumstances we cannot use the Bank of Canada for the purpose of creating money without any greater danger of inflation, thereby saving the people of Canada millions upon millions of dollars in interest.
With some members the term " inflation " has become an obsession; it is like waving a red rag in front of a bull. They are afraid to feed starving people for fear that those people will eat so much that they will burst. In other words, they are afraid to give money to starving people to buy the goods that are available for fear that they will buy so many that there will be a resulting shortage. Now, we fully realize that there is a well-defined limit to the amount of money that can be issued in any period, and so long as it does not go beyond that limit there need not be any fear of inflation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: What is the limit?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
The limit is the amount of money necessary to make the great physical demand of the people effective against the production of the country; that is to say, if you have on the one hand goods unsold and on the other hand people requiring those goods, you can give them enough money to buy those goods without any possible danger of inflation. There may be a danger of
Loan of $750,000,000

exploitation. Industry might say, " Seeing that there is more money in circulation we will take advantage of that fact to raise prices." But that is a matter for government control. In England during the war it was necessary for the government to exercise such control. The day that war was declared prices started to go up without any increase in the money in circulation, simply because industries wanted to exploit the people. The government therefore took action. That is not inflation but exploitation, and the government, will always have to take the necessary action to avoid it if prosperity is to be brought about by an increase in money.
Some members contend that if our argument is sound the system would have crashed long ago. I would point out that the system has been kept in operation by the creation of enormous unrepayable debts, bankruptcies and unnecesary starvation. I should like to give briefly two examples to show how the system has been kept in operation in the past. First, I would take a highly industrialized creditor nation, England, and secondly, the Dominion of Canada.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: What about Scotland?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: This will apply to Scotland as well as England. At any rate I am going to quote a Scotsman.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Be fair; call it Great Britain.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Very well, though he calls it England. I quote from Reginald McKenna, who I believe is a Scotsman, in a speech he made to the American Bankers' Association on October 5, 1922:
For over two centuries British capital, that is, credit, had been lent to other countries; year by year England produced more than she either consumed herself or could exchange for the products of other nations, and she could not obtain a market for the surplus unless she gave the purchaser a long credit. Foreign loans and foreign issues were taken up in England and the proceeds were spent in paying for the surplus production. British factories and workshops were kept in good employment, but it was a condition of their prosperity that a part of their output should be disposed of in this way.
That is to say, for over two hundred years England consumed only a portion of her production.

It does not give the date. It is quoted in this book. It must have been shortly after November, 1930, because it is a comment on this statement of Sir Samuel Martin. It reads:
Exporting is commonly referred to as though it were a thing desirable in itself; in fact, as we have often urged, the object of exporting is to create a credit abroad that can be used for the purchase of commodities, for permanent investment abroad, or for some other purpose; otherwise it is clear that the same need would be achieved if the goods were sent to sea and sunk in the Atlantic.
Yet that action, according to Reginald McKenna, brought prosperity to England. How much greater the resulting prosperity would have been if the money had been issued in the form of wages for public works, or in dividends, so that the people could have bought those goods, instead of giving the money to foreign nations to buy the goods and then having the debts repudiated.
I quote what Loftus has to say referring to this article:
It is difficult to bring home to the reader what this great loss of wealth has meant to the country. One may perhaps point out that all our great cities, London, Liverpool, Glasgow, Manchester, Birmingham and twenty or thirty more, could have been pulled down and rebuilt with wide streets, open spaces, parks and commodious healthy housing for all, with a portion of the wealth now as utterly lost to the nation as if. (to quote the Times,) it had been "sunk in the Atlantic."
This, I say, is a great condemnation of the system. But that is how it is kept in operation-by creating artificial scarcity in the country in which the goods are produced, and exporting to foreign nations. I contend that charity should begin at home.
I wish now to refer to what has happened in Canada under this system, going back prior to the war. Prior to 1914 there was in Canada fairly general prosperity, far better than we have now; men could always get a job. That prosperity was mainly due to the tremendous capital development that was taking place- the building of railways, highways, towns, and so on. The money so distributed in capital production was made available to the people to buy consumer goods. Prosperity was thus brought to Canada, but that prosperity was built on debt. To-day the people are being asked to pay in current prices not only the cost of production of current goods but also for the goods consumed prior to 1914. The wages, salaries and dividends paid out on current production cannot possibly by themselves pay for the production of former years, therefore the effective demand of the people against production to-day is being destroyed. The only way that can be made up is by issuing debt free money. If it is made up by borrowing, when the loan is repaid it has to be included in the price of the goods, and the same condition will result. We cannot pay debt with debt. We can transfer a debt from one place to another-

and interest free. Under our proposals, if at any time too much money was in circulation, it would be taken out of circulation, either by taxation or through the price discount factor. It would be taken out in order to avoid inflation, and could be cancelled or burnt as soon as taken out. This government taxes in order to get revenue for itself; we do not believe that is necessary. This government can issue what money is needed through the Bank of Canada. If too much money is in circulation, that money can be taxed out for the purpose of avoiding inflation, but not to

provide revenue. This government ties its activities down to the amount it can take from the people in taxes. The minister said that the only money available is what is taken from the people; we say that is a major factor in creating poverty, and absolutely unnecessary.

As I have already stated, to avoid this difficulty the Minister of Finance proposes that we must misappropriate the funds of the future. That is the only word I can use. We have no right to use the purchasing power of future generations for that purpose. What right have we to tell unborn generations: You have to pay a higher price for the goods you want in order that we may buy more goods to-day? It is rank dishonesty, a straight case of misappropriation of other people's funds.

Yes, absolutely, but I am not saying that any hon. member of this house is dishonest. I do not want anyone to think for a moment that I am suggesting that the Minister of Finance or anyone else is dishonest. I say we are operating under a dishonest system; that is the distinction I draw. When I attack the banking system as being a gigantic racket, I do not want anyone to think I am attacking the bankers, or accusing them of being dishonest men. I agree that the general run of bankers are as fine a body of men as any; it is not their fault that they are operating under a dishonest system. We maintain that so long as we continue to operate under this debt creating system our debts are bound to increase steadily year after year, resulting in increased taxation and increased poverty.
We therefore believe that internal expenditures can be met by national money, without any danger of inflation, provided that we are

only stimulating the demands of the people up to the capacity of industry to satisfy those demands.
Last year the Minister of Finance stated that an issue of money by the Bank of Canada might cause inflation, due to the practice of the chartered banks of expanding their loans up to ten times the amount of their cash. The minister used that as an argument against the issue of money by the Bank of Canada. I ask the minister, has parliament to-day established effective control over currency and credit?

Parliament through instruments which it has created and which are now in operation does control currency and credit in Canada day by day, week by week and month by month.
He is still of the same opinion. It is rather strange, though, that a few days after that statement was made the deputy governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. J. A. C. Osborne, speaking before the junior board of trade of Ottawa, should say:

In other words we control it only provided that our policy is acceptable to the Bank of Canada.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance told us last evening, and he has told us again, that he considers that this government has control of currency and credit; yet last year in this house he made a statement that showed absolutely beyond any shadow of doubt that we have no effective control of the issue of currency and credit in this country. Speaking on March 8, 1938, and referring to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) that we should issue some S350,000,000 for public works, the minister said:
An increase of say $350,000,000 in chartered bank holdings of Bank of Canada notes would increase their cash reserves from the present figure of about $250,000,000 to $600,000,000, and their cash ratio from about ten per cent to roughly twenty-four per cent.
The sponsor of the suggestion contends that no inflation is intended or would result by thus increasing bank cash, so long as the gold cover of the Bank of Canada did not fall below the twenty-five per cent minimum. This factor, however, is not a test of inflation. If the banks use their increased cash in a normal way, as a basis for the extension of roughly ten times as much in loans to the public, or for the acquisition of ten times as much in investments, bank deposits would expand by approximately an equal amount until the cash ratio was brought down again to approximately ten per cent. This would mean an increase in bank deposits from the present level of about $2,387,000,000 to something like $6,000,000,000, or more than 2'6 times the level of December 31, 1929.
Then he goes on to say:
Am I merely old fashioned or orthodox when I say that this would mean a colossal measure of inflation?

The laws of King Alfred, about 900 A.D., directed that the effects of money lenders upon usury should be forfeited to the king, their lands to the lords under whom they were held, and they should not be buried in consecrated ground.
By the laws of Edward the Confessor, about 1050 A.D., the usurer forfeited all his property and was declared an outlaw and banished from England. In the reign of Henry II, about the close of the twelfth century, the estates of usurers were forfeited at their death and their children were disinherited.
His successor, Richard I, was yet more severe, forbidding the usurers attending his coronation, nor would he protect them from mob violence.
During the thirteenth century the severities against the usurers were not relaxed. King John confiscated their gathered wealth without scruples.
In the fourteenth century, under the three Edwards, the taking of interest was an indictable offence and Edward III made it a capital crime.

Well, Mr. Chairman, we are in committee; the discussion will continue.
I shall not attempt to make any longer statement just now, but I wanted to touch the high spots of the proposal. I think the committee can see it. It is a proposal to inflate the volume of existing currency two and a half to four and a half times its present volume, and to use that currency to pay off the obligations of the dominion as they mature within the next two years. That in my judgment is absolutely uncontrolled inflation of the crudest possible variety. In my judgment it would ruin the credit of this dominion, would bring misery and suffering, particularly to our poorest people, would give opportunities to the speculatively minded to make and lose fortunes, would bring about precisely what has happened all through history whenever that kind of thing has been tried, whether by kings of old or in more recent years in some of the countries of Europe. It seems a pity that each succeeding generation has to learn the lesson afresh. It is indeed bitter experience. We do not find similar measures being proposed in any country which has had recent experience of them.
For the moment I shall confine myself to questioning the order of the amendment, in that it changes completely the scheme of the original resolution. I do not deny that my hon. friend can alter his amendment and put it in order, and I shall be glad to have him do so; or he can withdraw it, as he wishes.

speechtext: I should like to have it redrafted in proper form, and it can then be presented.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Very well. I should like this committee to go on record in this matter. We want to make known to the people of Canada and the people of the world whether we want to embark on crude and uncontrolled inflation, or whether we will maintain that measure of scientific control which has been made possible by the creation of the Bank of Canada and by the various statutes of this country dealing with the control of currency and credit. I said last year that in my opinion we have now under our present statutes an ample measure of control of currency and credit. The only question is, and it is a difficult and serious one: How shall we use the degree of control which we have, from day to day, from week to week, from month to month? We take the view that the control must be used carefully, having regard at all times to one interest only, the best interest of all the people of Canada; taking into account all the various conditions which must be con-
Loan oj $750,000,000

sidered in connection with this most difficult question of control of currency and credit. It is more difficult to-day as a world question than it has ever been before, because of the abandonment by most of the nations of the world of that standard which rendered things a great deal easier to manage during a long period of years. We have now, as I said the other day, management of credit and currency in all countries, not by an agreed-upon gold standard, but management by men's minds, by the thinking of those who are placed in control of credit and currency. The standard which worked for so many years of agreed-upon international value for gold is for the time being suspended, therefore we have the variable factor that in each country groups of men entrusted by government with the task are endeavouring to manage their credit and currency in the interests of their own people. Under these circumstances how much greater is the difficulty of bringing about that international understanding which makes trade relations between nations possible and sound.
I say again, as I said the other day, that for Canada-fourth exporting nation in the world, fifth in total trade in the world, with the relations which she must have with other countries-for Canada to embark on uncontrolled inflation of credit or currency or both, would in my opinion be national suicide.

speechtext:
Yes; I should like to make a few remarks while the hon. member for Calgary East is redrafting his amendment. I am not sure, but it looks as though after three and a half years this is to be the first time we have really been able to come to grips; and, Mr. Chairman, may I say that if we all play the rules and keep our heads we may get quite a little way with this discussion.
In the first place I wish to point out one or two things as we see them. The Minister of Finance insists on declaring on every occasion that the Social Credit party advocates inflation. I say we do not.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: What is it?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Manifestly the first thing to do is to define " inflation," because I believe there exists in this parliament and throughout the dominion the wildest degree of uncertainty, inaccuracy of information and, I may say, prejudice concerning the word. What is inflation? Not only is it inflation; it is called crude inflation, though not one member from this group has ever advocated either inflation or crude inflation. Time and again the minister has also used the words " uncontrolled inflation." One cannot advocate the creation of ten dollars of dominion money without its being called uncontrolled inflation, crude inflation or simply inflation. What contemptible piffle! All one needs to do is recall that between 1915 and 1917 the Dominion of Canada printed $26,000,000 of bills, of which $10,000,000 had nothing behind it and $16,000,000 had only worthless	railway
securities behind it. Apparently those bills were used for government purposes, and they did not cause inflation or disturb the exchanges. They were sound money then, and they have been sound money ever since. All one needs to do is remember that fact to see how absurd are some of these contentions, when people

Loan oj $750,000,000
call any issue of government money inflation, crude inflation or uncontrolled inflation. So I hope we shall not have to spend any more time talking about inflation, crude inflation or uncontrolled inflation, because this group advocates none of the three.
There is one other point I wish to get quite clear. As far as I can remember, never since we came to this house have we refused to answer a question which has been put to us.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Yes, you have, many times.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

I can say that personally I have never done so; I defy any member of the house to point to any occasion when I refused. Time and again I have tried to secure the privilege of asking a question in order to correct a false impression which was being created in the course of a speech; in over half of the cases I have been refused, many times with insults from the opposite side. I just ask if that is what they consider fair play. We will permit any number of questions and try to answer them. If we cannot answer them, it is evident that we simply do not know the answers, but we should like the privilege of asking questions in turn. If we are to be denied that privilege, let it be known; let the country know that here is a group that is not allowed the privilege of asking questions. We are supposed to be ignoramuses; we are not supposed to know what we are talking about. Why be afraid of answering any questions that we can devise?
Now I am going to spend a few moments on the subject of inflation. What is inflation? I am going to quote two authorities in that regard, and I think it will take a good deal to explain them away. Before I do so, however, let me say this: You do not have inflation in a country until you have more money coming into the markets of that country to buy than there are goods and services to be bought with that money, without a rise in prices.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
One thing at a time, please. That is a definition of inflation; just as soon as you get more money in circulation than you have goods and services to be bought with that money, without a rise in prices, then you have inflation. It matters not whether the government creates that money, whether a banker creates it, or whether it comes in from outside the country. Let us get that laid down solidly as a fundamental principle.
Before I quote the authorities I mentioned a moment ago, I should like to point out something in which I believe all hon. members will be interested. On November 13, 1933, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) delivered a speech in Toronto, of which I have a copy in my hand. One thing he said has a bearing on this subject. In the course of his remarks the hon. member made clear to his audience that between 1929 and 1933 the banking fraternity in the Dominion of Canada withdrew from circulation some $932,000,000. There is no question that this was a most colossal deflation. The people after that were without the money that was necessary to carry on business, and as a result prices fell and disaster reigned generally throughout the country. But, according to the definition of inflation which apparently is in the minds of most hon. members, if the government of the day had undertaken to put $100,000,000 of that huge amount back into circulation it would have been inflation, crude inflation, uncontrolled inflation. What nonsense!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

I am glad to hear it is not so; we will have a discussion on that later on.
I quote these facts so that we may come to grips with the problem in a general way. It is not likely, Mr. Chairman, that a whole province of this dominion would go completely crazy over an idea so fallacious as the Minister of Finance would lead us to suppose this is.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

In all probability it
will be found that the people of Alberta could give some very good reasons for the hope that is within them.
Now, first of all, with respect to inflation I am going to quote a passage from Planned Money by Sir Basil P. Blackett, published in 1932. This very short quotation appears at page 106. I would ask hon. members to note it carefully:
The right amount of currency in circulation at any given moment is that amount which will do the work required of it at a given level of prices. If it is too much, prices will rise. If it is too little, they will fall.
The minute you get more money in circulation, let me repeat, than enough to do the work of distributing goods and services which are abroad in a country to be distributed, then you have inflation, and not a minute before.

speechtext:
It matters not who creates the money, or where it comes from. This idea of trying to foist upon the people of this country and the world the idea that a dollar of dominion money backed by the credit of this dominion is inflation, while a dollar created by the most insignificant bank manager is sound money, is nonsense in the highest degree.
I shall quote another statement by a man who surely is respected in his country- whether in this country, or not. I refer to Senator Owen, who is prominent in monetary affairs in the United States. His ideas are not entirely popular, but neither were the ideas of the great inventors, the great reformers or the great leaders of times past in other great movements. But they were right, just the same. Here is what Senator Owen said when giving evidence on June 9, 1937 before a committee of the United States senate in connection with a discussion on "Farm Commodity Prices":
Inflation does not occur until maximum employment and production is achieved. If it should occur, the volume of money could be immediately reduced by selling bonds, by sales tax and other taxes, and retiring such excess money from circulation.
I ask any hon. member of the house: After the $932,000,000 was withdrawn from circulation in Canada, do you suppose there was enough money in the country to do the business of the country? Certainly not. The government at that time could easily have created money and put it into circulation without getting into circulation more than enough money to do the business of the country. That is abundantly clear. Never from that day to this has there been a sufficient restoration of the money that was withdrawn in those four years-never yet. Until enough money is restored to circulation you cannot speak of inflation with any degree of understanding or sincerity.

Yes, I grant that,- and that is just the sort of question and answer I welcome. I shall gladly answer questions from hon. members. It has been the contention of this group steadily that purchasing power is of two kinds, both currency and credit. So far as its ability to buy and do other work is concerned, I think my hon. friend will admit that every dollar of the $932,000,000 could do just as much work as a dollar bill. The result was that when that credit was withdrawn the country was short of money, just as definitely as though it had been dollar bills. I am glad the minister raised that point, and let me get it straight.
Now, dollar bills might be replaced by either credit or currency. The minister made much of a further point-and he is sincere when he makes a statement. I am just as sincere when I say he is wrong. The clash between the two of us on the issue is there, and perfectly honestly. He says that when one dollar is drawn from circulation somebody has to pay for it. We do not doubt that. Every dollar he withdraws by taxation now somebody has to pay for. Surely. But if the dollar he withdraws from taxation happens to have been borrowed out of a bank, and then withdrawn by him through taxation, there are at least two people paying that dollar, the man who has to pay it back to the bank and the man who has to pay it in to the government. There is no escaping the truth of that statement.
There are a great many people in the country who have the idea that you cannot have a dollar unless it is a debt dollar. I ask any hon. member: What about that $26,000,000 that Canada created? Was that debt money? Did anybody do anything for that money? Did it cost this dominion one cent? Was it paid back? The answer in every single case must be no. There was some debt free money and there was some interest free money, beyond any question.
The minister implied that every time in the world's history a government has issued money it has gone awry. He did not use those words and, while I do not wish to overstate what he has said, yet on the other hand wish to be perfectly honest, I believe I have interpreted him correctly. His implication was that whenever a government has created and used state money we have had crude or uncontrolled inflation and disastrous consequences.

speechtext: That is the principle to which I object. The Guernsey island people did not do that. I shall speak further of that experiment when I have a little more time, and it will likely be in this debate. The first move of the Guernsey island people was to create three thousand one-pound notes, and with those build a market house. Then it collected the three thousand one-pound notes as yearly dues on the market place, and no one owed anybody for the money. The state created it and the state spent it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: And the taxpayers paid it back.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Surely. Very fine. But the difficulty is that if Canada had been doing that, Canada would have borrowed the three thousand pounds from a banker and then would have taxed the people enough to pay it all back to the banker, and to pay the interest on it as well, and still the people and the government would have owed the bank the three thousand pounds. That is exactly where thr difference lies. I think that is quite clear
Loan oj $750,000,000

Without discussing money further now, I am going to say a word or two about the debt situation in Canada. I expected to say something about that, but I was not quite sure whether I would be allowed to speak on it. Until recently I thought I knew a little about the rules of the house, but now I find I know practically nothing about them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Why not wait for the budget debate?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Then we would not have time to discuss this matter. I may seem over-earnest in discussing money, but it is the most important thing that you can discuss to-day; for this proposal will work out a solution of your problems, which otherwise are unsolvable. To relegate the discussion of this vitally important matter to some little corner does not appeal to us as common sense. Let me say that we have deliberately refrained from participating in many of the discussions of this house so that in the time which might justly be allowed to us we could set forth the message that we came here to deliver. All we want is an opportunity to set it forth and an attentive, patient hearing such as we give to those who are speaking of other matters.
Now just a word about Canada's debt.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Before my hon. friend goes to debt-

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Goes into debt.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Before my hon. friend goes into the subject of debt, may I ask him this question? If he were putting into effect in Canada a new monetary system along the lines he is advocating, would it still be a principle of that system that I could go to a clearing house or some other institution and obtain there a credit which I, in turn, could use for the purpose of acquiring goods without my giving to that institution, in exchange for that credit, either goods or services or a promise to deliver goods or services at some future date? I ask that sincerely because 1 am anxious to understand.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
That, of course, is a sincere question. In order to be able to understand it, I must first lay down this principle, that social credit has two great objectives in the financial system. The first one of these is to see to it that there is adequate production of all kinds, sufficient to the needs of all the people of Canada. The second of these is to bring about consumption. The money which is advanced for production goes, as it does to-day, in the form of a debt, and it must be repaid.
[Mr. Blackmoro.J

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me, is it not conceded by all people that we have all the production that we can possibly need in Canada, and that our need is not greater production but the power to consume what we are producing and an equitable distribution of the profits of that production? I am trying to follow the hon. member.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Yes, but the reason I stated that principle first for my hon. friend is that if we said, first of all, that we will issue money for consumption, then we would be met at once by the very thing that popped up when we first came to parliament, when an hon. member who is now in the chamber said: We cannot produce enough.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Still true.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
There, do you hear that? You see how it directly opposes what the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson) said. So we say the first thing is to make sure that you will have all of the production that all of your people can use in so far as your resources and the industrial equipment which you possess can produce that abundance; and you govern that by lending, perhaps at two per cent or one and a half per cent interest, whatever amount is necessary to bring down the cost of production where it ought to be, instead of where it is to-day. That is the first principle to be grasped. That money continues to go out as a debt; but still, so far as the government is concerned, it is not a debt. That is, the government does not borrow it from anyone, does not owe anyone for it.
Some people may say: We do not understand that. Perhaps in this very discussion I will bring to the attention of the committee the treasury note, the Bradbury, in England, and will point out the way in which the British people managed to get into circulation over three hundred million pounds of paper that did not cost the British treasury one cent beyond the cost of printing the notes.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I would ask the hon. member if he has answered the question put by the hon. member for York South in the affirmative or in the negative.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Just as soon as we can get to it. Let us not rush along. As the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) so well pointed out, the social credit concept is this. There is at the present time in our financial and productive system a deficiency of purchas-

Loan oj $750,000,000
ing power. This is well illustrated by the figures which record United States production and income in 1918. In that year, as is shown in Income of the United States, volume 2, pages 242 to 248, there were sixty billion dollars' worth of consumers' goods produced, and into the hands of the consumers in wages, salaries, dividends, bonuses and every other form of purchasing power, there went only forty-five billion dollars. The result was that there were fifteen billion dollars' worth of consumers' goods which there was no purchasing power in the hands of the people to buy. The result was that either the goods had to be sold on time or credit, putting the people of the United States into debt, or they had to be sold to foreign nations, putting them into debt. That is the very principle about which the hon. member for Acadia was talking a few minutes ago. It was considered sound finance for the government of the United States to advance credits to foreign countries- let us say, for fifteen billion dollars, although of course that is too much-to let them buy those goods on time; but to advance the credit to their own people has never yet entered their minds.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: If my hon. friend will pardon me-I know what he is telling us, because I have taken the trouble to try to make a study of the social credit system-if the United States lends money to a foreign nation it gets that nation's promise to pay, be it good, bad or indifferent, and that is in effect a promise to deliver future goods and services. If the social credit monetary system is put into effect, do I understand that the hon. member advocates the advance of credit- which according to him is as good as money- to people without those people in turn delivering, in exchange for that credit, goods or services, or without their promise to deliver at some future time goods or services?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: We are coming right to the answer.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: You are a long time coming.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Well, I may have to be.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Not for me.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
It so happens that the hon. member for York South is a little keener than a good many other hon. members. I have had some experience with some of them. I come now to the direct answer to my hon. friend's question. Suppose we keep in mind the situation in the United States. If the United States, with sixty billion dollars' worth of consumers' goods in 1918, 71492-97
realizing it has only forty-five billion dollars with which to buy the goods, wishes to balance its economy to enable its producers to sell their goods, what must it do?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Issue more medium of
exchange.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Now we are on the right track. Exactly. That is the social credit contention. Just as an illustration, let me come back to Canada and the twenty-six million dollars.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: A minute ago the hon. member said "billions," and now he says "millions."

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: If I made a slip I stand corrected. I am listening to all these questions at the same time and trying to get through a speech.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: We are trying to follow you.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: That is all right. We will get there. At least I hope so, in the interests of Canada and the British empire. When Canada created that twenty-six million dollars, was it necessary that that money should be lent out only to somebody who agreed to pay it back, or could it have been used to pay soldiers' pensions or widows' pensions or pensions for the blind or the aged? There is no conceivable reason why it could not have been used as a gift to the people. It would have been just as good, just as sound money.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Oh, yes, but-if my hon. friend will pardon me-surely he will agree with me that if we take this money or currency or credit and use it as a gift to somebody, that simply means that we are arbitrarily taking from somebody else something which is theirs in order to give it to another class.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Not necessarily.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: We are redistributing goods and services without something being given in exchange.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Let us keep right to the point. I appreciate greatly the interest; that is what we want. I want to answer the first question, and I am going to put the matter straightforwardly. I say unqualifiedly, yes, the government will create the purchasing power which is necessary to market this fifteen billion dollars' worth of goods in the United States. It will distribute that purchasing power to the people, who will buy the goods, and thereby enable the producers

Loan of $750,000,000

to have a market and assist their economy to go forward, and equate consumption with production.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Without the people who receive it giving goods or services in return?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Yes, unquestionably.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I cannot quite hear.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

The money would be
given without any return?

speechtext:
In a way it seems
queer. This is new to us, I know; but Mr. Chairman, I ask you, can we expect a new system which will solve our problems to be devoid of something which is new and strange to us? Everything else about us is new and strange; why shall we not expect the solution of our problems to involve and embody principles which are new and strange?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: If my hon. friend permits me, we all admire his system, but what we want to know is how it will work.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
May I go back to
the question of the hon. member for York South? I had not expected to talk along this line, so I am speaking quite extemporaneously. I trust I do not make a slip which will be reported in Hansard, it is easy to do so when one is speaking extemporaneously.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: The hon. member is making himself perfectly clear.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I want to make
myself perfectly clear. I think I can do so without making statements which can be distorted. But I am anxious to make myself clear at this point although just now I had not been thinking it through. I have gone through it scores of times, but not upon the floor of the house before such an interested audience.
As the hon. member for Acadia pointed out, what did Great Britain do? She advanced millions of pounds on credit so that she could sell her goods, and she thought it was good business. She lost money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: But she had the promise to pay.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
She got in exchange the
promise to deliver goods and services of an equivalent value in the future.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
She got nothing for
the promises. But she was not ruined. What she got was a market.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
She got or expected to
get her money back.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Those are losses over
a long period.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Exactly. But the
money never came back.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Not that particular
money. But other money did.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Perhaps, but a great
deal has not come back. To continue point by point; this is a new idea; we grant that. I wonder if I have answered the hon. member for York South?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
You have answered my
original question completely, in the affirmative.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Now we are dealing
with the logicality of the proposal. Is it logical; is it sensible to give money to people to buy with? That is the next question. Let us refer to the fifteen billion dollars of surplus goods. Is it logical to let fifteen billion dollars' worth of goods be destroyed?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Is it logical to let
those goods stay on the shelves until they decay? Is it logical to let the factories which produced them close up and to turn men out of work so that they can no longer produce goods?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Monetize the goods.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Is it logical to issue millions of dollars of debt which will never be paid? That is what we are doing. Is it logical to engage in a trade war with other countries, trying to elbow other countries out of foreign markets so that we can sell our goods, against-for instance-the competition of the United States, thereby engaging in an international trade war which may ultimately lead to armed conflict? These are things which have been done up to the present time. Social creditors say that such foolish and wasteful practices are all absolutely illogical, absolutely insane, and that they must be changed. What the United States needed above all other things, when they had sixty billion dollars' worth of goods and only forty-five billion dollars' worth of purchasing power, was another fifteen billion dollars' worth of purchasing power, fifteen billion dollars' worth of markets whereby those goods could be put

Loan oj S750,000,000
into the hands of the people. The thing we are suffering from is simply this, that after we have installed the machine to produce shoes, for example, without the use of manpower, the men who are displaced are unable to obtain shoes. We cannot get the shoes into the hands of the poor fellows who, because they have been displaced, are unable to earn wages.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: It is easy to get the shoes into their hands. All you have to do is give it to them, and that is more simple than the hon. member's' scheme. AVhat I say sincerely is that, having tried to study his scheme, I have come to the conclusion that that is exactly what he proposes to accomplish, namely, to give the shoes away for nothing. They give nothing in exchange. They do not give any goods or services in exchange, and if they do not, what are they going to give?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: In exchange, they are giving consumption. Men are coming to realize that a person who can consume is an asset to a country. Let any agent to-day, representing any company, go out and try to sell his product. What is the first thing he does in the community in which he is trying to promote sales? He looks for men who might be able to buy.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Effective buyers; that is, those who have something to give in exchange.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: That is why we need purchasing power.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: But when someone is not an effective buyer and consumes anyway, he is not an asset but a liability.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Let us study the question calmly-

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I did not mean to interrupt the hon. gentleman.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: We welcome interruptions. That is what we want. Let us take the questions point by point, answering one at a time even if we have to stay here all night-because we can answer all these questions.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: What about the resolution?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Suppose the dominion government creates a five dollar bill and puts it into the hands of a widow, enabling her to buy a pair of shoes. The government is not exactly compelling the shoe factory to give her a pair of shoes.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
But we are making the people of Canada give it to her, the people from whom we take five dollars by way of taxation.
71492-97J

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: You are not making the people of Canada give it so long as you have not created more purchasing power than there are goods and services to justify the giving of that five dollars.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I cannot agree with your premise.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: It is true whether you agree with it or not. When you have in the United States $15,000,000,000 worth of consumers' goods which you cannot sell, those goods are a justification for the creation of more money, and the state can create more money up to the extent to which it can enable the people to consume or distribute the $15,000,000,000 worth of goods. And there will not be any inflation, according to the definitions of that word which I have read from Sir Basil Blackett. If there is no inflation you take nothing from the people because there is no rise in prices as a result of which there is any indirect taxation. If new money results in a rise in prices, creating an indirect tax, then you are taking something from the people. But if you create a new dollar bill, which does not cause inflation, and put it into the hands of a person who has to consume, you have created a market in your own country and distributed the product in your own country, and you have blessed both your own consumers and your own producers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Then why should anyone work if he can get something without working? Why should any man work if he can get purchasing power for what he needs without having to go to work? And what would happen to production if everybody said, " There is no need to work because we can get purchasing power without doing so?"

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: That is an excellent question.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Answer it.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Hon. members will notice that we have changed our point of discussion from inflation to an altogether different aspect of the subject.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I was never on inflation; that is not a bugbear to me.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Now we are on the question, how to get the people to work under the system that we propose. My time has already gone, and the chairman has been considerate enough to give me some latitude. I must hurry. That is a legitimate question and it must be answered. Suppose the government gave $25 a month to everyone-I mention that figure because everyone hears about $25 to-day-and that there were jobs
Loan oj $750,000,000

to be had. Now take any young couple, a married couple, say. The young woman gets $25 and her husband gets $25.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

speechtext:
(Temis-couaita): I 'have listened with deep interest to the last part of the speech delivered by the leader of the Social Credit party (Mr. Black-more). There are some points in his speech which I do not understand, and I will try to give him an explanation of what I gather from his remarks. I will try to be just as courteous as he has been, and to answer to the best of my ability any questions that may come from his group. I am not a mathematician and I will not deal in large figures-billions or trillions. I will speak only of millions. That is large enough for concrete examples of what we understand.

In the first place, at a time when the happiness of man was unclouded, in the garden of Eden, there was no mint to make currency. Man was happy just the same. After Adam and Eve were expelled from the garden of Eden, it was a penalty imposed upon them, to earn their own living. But for several centuries there was no coinage. It was the wonderful age of the patriarchs; they had no coins although they exchanged goods. It is just on account of the fact that our great-great-great-great-great-grandparents were expelled from the garden of Eden because of their sin that man has to work and to receive money for his services or his work. Therefore coinage is the result of sin.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

To speak in another vein, of course there is only one Christmas in the year. In order to give money freely to people there should be beforehand a very important reform, a reform of the calendar. Instead of one Christmas only, we should have Christmases every day of the year.

speechtext:
I know my hon. friends are sincere; I do not mistrust their sincerity. But when people have no money, I wonder whether it is wise to speak to them of millions without giving millions to them. Those who are thirsty it makes more thirsty, and those who are hungry it makes more hungry. It is dangerous to show bubbles to the people. They are brilliant, but they disappear very soon.
There is the question of the creation of purchasing power. What is it? It is power to purchase, or the power to get some other goods. For what consideration, or how shall

Loan oj $750,000,000
we get it? There is a Latin line which is known by all: Quis, quid, ubi, cur, quibus auxiliis, quomodo, quando? Whenever there is an argument of some kind one can ask, Quis-who said it? I know it is Major Douglas who first said it, and he had some eminent disciples in this country, including the premier of Alberta. They are highly respectable people, we know, and they say it. Then there is quid; What do they say? On that point I am not sure because I do not understand very well. Then there is quod; Why?
I do not impute motives to anyone, and I shall not say that it is for political motives. Quibus auxiliis? With what help, what assistance? Is it with the assistance of the provincial government of Alberta, or people of goodwill throughout this country who are ready to subscribe any amount of money to see the result of experience? It may be possible. Then there is also quomodo? by what means; and quando? when. I know of course that the theory is expounded to us and explained very ably, but to my mind not absolutely satisfactorily. Therefore the main points are: What is it, how will it be done, and when? I leave aside the other questions.
It is a law of nature that man has to work to earn his living. In the first place there was no coinage; there was no money; man worked and he received clothes and food from his employer. Those who were rich exchanged cattle for other goods, until trade became more widespread and cities came into being; then every man could not have a herd of camels or sheep or other animals to dispose of in order to obtain other things that he required, and people becoming more civilized got some form of coinage, which as my hon. friends know was first a piece of stone, which was supposed to have value. At that tame the population of the world was not so big, but when the population became larger it was understood by tradesmen that they had to exchange a certain quantity of metal for other goods that they required for their living.

speechtext: I thank the hon. member for Lethbridge warmly for his kind words. Perhaps he would tell me how A or B may be given any purchasing power in the form of money by the state for services that are not rendered, except by w'ay of a gratuity voted by both houses of parliament and sanctioned by the governor general?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I think this will cover that point. The dominion government to-day is granting relief to the extent of millions of dollars and is getting no services in return. If the dominion government can borrow money or raise money by taxation and give that money to people without getting a return for it, is there any reason why they should not be able to create money and do the same thing with it? If by borrowing money now the government are able to give a man $25, $30 or $40 a month-which is not enough -is there any reason why, if the production of the country will justify it, they should not create enough money to give that man $50, which might be somewhere near what he ought to have?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
The government subscribes some money for the relief of a certain group of good Canadians who unfortunately have no means of earning their livelihood. That
Loan oj 8750,000,000

is true, but that group does not include all Canadians. Those who receive this assistance form only a fraction of our population, and this relief is paid by the taxes which come from the pockets of the rest of the population, as my hon. friend knows. On the other hand, if every Canadian is to receive $25 or $50 a month, who will pay for it? That is my point. If the Canadian parliament has decided, on humanitarian grounds, to give assistance in the form of relief or relief works to that portion of the population which is unemployed, my hon. friend must remember that this is only one part and not the whole population. Furthermore, as my hon. friend knows very well, if everyone were assisted by parliament there would be no more relief. It would be a kind of superannuation for everyone in this country, by means of money voted by parliament.
Suppose we have a group of one hundred people forming the whole population of the world. Of the one hundred two are sick and five are unemployed. These seven are assisted by the remaining ninety-three, out of charity.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: What about the machines?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I am answering the hon. member for Lethbridge. If any other hon. member desires to ask me a question he may do so. Seven of the one hundred are assisted by the ninety-three remaining. But suppose each of the one hundred receives $25 a month. Would that come from the pocket of A to the pocket of B and from B back to A? Is it just an exchange of money that comes from somewhere else? And if these one hundred people, forming the population of the world, were all unemployed, how would they get $25 or S50 a month or a week?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
That is a sincere question, and I think I can bring the answer forcibly to the hon. member's attention in this way: If we continue at our present rate we shall arrive at the point where all the goods and services people can possibly use will be produced by about two per cent of the population. So that really the people who are getting the S50 a month are getting it from the work of the machines, which have so tremendously increased the productive power of our people that it is almost as though we had these hundred people in a lovely valley where all the fruits, all the fishes and everything of that kind were produced in abundance. We know such conditions could exist. We have virtually made this wTorld into such a valley now where we can produce plenty; for we have learned to produce more of every kind of food, clothing, shelter and amusement, than we can use.

But we cannot use the labour of all the people; we use machines instead. The question is, shall we let the machines work and let the people have the results of that work, much as one would allow people to pick fruit from the hillsides and catch fish in the streams; or shall we deny all the people who cannot get at the machines the privilege of enjoying any of the benefits derived from the machines which put them out of w'ork? That is the vital question confronting us.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
