speechtext: Therefore, of the one hundred only two would work, and they would have to provide that $25 a week for the ninety-eight others. This would mean that these two men would have to provide over $100,000 for the support of the ninety-eight others. Each man would require a salary of about $50,000 to give away for the benefit of the others.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: My hon. friend is overlooking the work done by the machines; he has not allowed for that. There are just two men managing the machines, and the machines are doing the work. You can get an illustration of that by going to a power plant. After the plant is completed, two or three men can run it and produce all the power needed over a wide area. The power plant is there and is producing this service out of the resources of the country, and the resources and machinery of the country belong to the state, to the people as a whole. That is beyond any question, just as our highways, churches, schools and universities belong to the people, even though those who built and paid for them may be dead. Do I answer the question?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I do not think my hon. friend has met the point. There are a hundred men together. Only two of those men have purchasing power. In other words, two have to support ninety-eight others. My hon. friend mentioned that there could be a creation of purchasing power. I should like

Loan of $750,000,000
to know how we would increase the purchasing power of the ninety-eight people who have no money at all and no means of getting it?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: That is where the state comes in. If the machines operated by two men are producing enough shoes, food and eveiy other kind of goods to feed all of the one hundred, then it will be the state's task to turn the goods into money; for while goods ought to be purchasing power, to-day they are not purchasing power unless they can be sold. The goods must be changed into money before they become genuine purchasing power. The state, using goods, creates purchasing power, tickets, and distributes them to the men, and then the men are able to take part of that supply of goods. That is the kind of situation we are going into, beyond doubt. It is not a question of the amount of income each of the two men can win running the machines. It is the fact that the products of the machines are enough to supply everybody's needs and are changed into purchasing power in the form of money or tickets, as though the machines were creating a great heap of all kinds of goods, and all the people around were enabled to have a share out of the pile. The tickets are made and distributed to the people so that they can buy goods out of the pile. If that is not done you will find this peculiar thing happening: With the two men doing all the work and apparently having all the purchasing power, your machines will run just long enough to feed the two men, while all the others will starve and the machines will stand idle-which would be absurd.

maintopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: To the best of my knowledge I may have said what the hon. member has quoted. I was interpreting section 8 of the original charter of 1895 which provides for the use by the company of "any approved mechanical power or other means, agency or force for such purpose that science or invention may develop." I certainly used the words "that science or invention may develop," if that is what my hon. friend is referring to, because those are the words used in the original charter of 1895.

maintopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend for his explanation, but if he is correctly reported there is no need for this bill. He is proposing that the original charter be amended to permit the company to use buses, but if the original charter covers whatever forms of transportation science may develop the present bill is useless.
I should like to summarize what has happened in this case. It is to be regretted at times that the evidence which is given before all the committees of the house is not recorded. Able counsel for the Quebec Railway company, after numerous questions had been put to them, admitted in the committee that the company was operating buses; that it was also operating taxis, and further, that it controlled the majority of shares in the Quebec

Cartage Company. The Quebec Cartage Company is a taxi and truck company, and therefore they do not need this legislation at all. In other words, the Quebec Railway Company comes here just to be in a position to state that the Quebec utilities commission has no jurisdiction over the rates that the company may charge the travelling public, and this bill is just a smoke-screen. I do not see how the committee can approve it. That is my first point.
But there are other considerations. The agreement between the railway company and the city of Quebec is one that apparently requires approval by the dominion parliament. At least six or eight times there have been previous agreements between the city of Quebec and the Quebec Railway company, but at none of these times did both parties come to parliament for approval. They went to the Quebec legislature, and I do not see why they do not follow the same procedure now. There is no reason for changing their procedure, because we have no jurisdiction whatever in such matters.
May I remind the committee of another statement which was made by Mr. J. A. Nadeau, chief counsel for the city of Quebec, before the railway committee. He was asked if it was the intention of the city to have the same exclusive franchise for buses as they have already for trolley cars for a period of thirty years from 1925 to 1955, and he answered affirmatively. That, of course, is outside the knowledge of hon. members who have not attended the sittings of the railway committee.
Therefore, sir, because this parliament has no jurisdiction over buses that operate within one province only, and because the purpose of the city of Quebec is to secure by this disguised legislation an exclusive franchise, it seems to me that this committee should not approve the bill.

their franchise and they now wish to operate trolley buses and auto buses. I am quite prepared to grant them that privilege, but they also wish to operate in addition "all kinds of public or private conveyances." I think that takes in a little too much territory. I do not understand why they should want to provide now for some sort of conveyance that may be operating five or six years from now under some different name from trolley bus or auto bus. It seems to me that if they get what they are asking for now, the right to operate trolley buses and auto buses, they should be quite satisfied with that. Then, in five or ten years' time, if there is some other sort of public conveyance for which they wish to have a franchise, they can come and get it. They have not offered me any reasonable excuse why they should ask for that. It is that to which I want to object, and to be on record as objecting to that clause: "all kinds of public or private conveyances."
If they are willing to delete that clause, I am quite willing that the bill should pass; otherwise I want my vote registered against it.

speechtext: We had to consider this whole question rather carefully when we undertook certain responsibilities in connection with youth training. It has already been announced that at this session of parliament a bill will be introduced to provide for a continuance of youth training over a period of three years, so that I should feel that in very large measure the government had responded to the opinion which, I agree, is prevalent in the country, that there is a need for technical education. maintopic: TECHNICAL EDUCATION

maintopic: TECHNICAL EDUCATION
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext: I think this question is above mere partisan polities. I understand that the youth training projects which this government contemplated and for which money has been voted have been sabotaged- I do not use the word in an offensive sense- by lack of cooperation on the part of the government of Ontario, and my information is that there is about $135,000 now available through the department which might be taken advantage of for youth training in technical education in Ontario. If I am in error in the figure the minister can correct me. It is obvious, it seems to me, that for some reason best known to themselves the government of Ontario are not receptive to the idea of using that money in the form in which it has been given for the training of youth in technical education in that province. I am confident that the minister is sincere in his desire to advance youth training and technical education, and I suggest that as an alternative to his present scheme, which apparently is resisted in Ontario-I do not know about the other provinces-he might very well consider the idea of going back to the original scheme of providing a fund on the basis of the original Technical Education Act, which might be taken advantage of in the provinces, and which, I believe, would be made use of in Ontario.

maintopic: TECHNICAL EDUCATION

speechtext:
I wonder if any of the money which the minister appears to have on hand under the vote for technical education could be used for aviation purposes. The Toronto board of education are anxious to extend their facilities for instruction in aviation. In 1932 or 1933, or earlier, the board commenced teaching matters pertaining to aviation in a branch of the technical school on Bathurst street. They now desire to branch out considerably because, as the minister knows, there is a large number of young men who would make first-class aviators, but unfortunately it is too expensive to teach them. A few days ago the board sent a letter to Ottawa asking the Toronto members to support their request for an increase in aviation facilities under the technical school grant. I assume that the minister has seen that communication and has been in touch with the board.
In the branch of the technical school located on Bathurst street the facilities are altogether inadequate for further advance in the subject. Is it possible to use some of this money to assist the board not only in the development of an aviation curriculum in the city but for the purpose of promoting cooperation in some way with one or more of the flying schools located in the vicinity of
(Mr. Rogers.]
Toronto? If that is not satisfactory, perhaps they could start flying courses themselves outside the city where students could finish their education as aviators. I do not know whether that conflicts with what the government is doing, at present. I understand that a few years ago a number of students who had obtained initial education in aviation in the Toronto technical school graduated either to Camp Borden or to Trenton. If some of the money could be used by the government for these purposes two very useful purposes would be served. In the first place, an opportunity would be afforded a good many young Canadians to learn aviation from the beginning, as I suppose they do now-that is, all about the machines, engines and so on. Second, provision would be made for turning out well trained young men for commercial aviation or perhaps for another form of flying which we hope will never be necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: TECHNICAL EDUCATION

It is quite true that the government has received requests from the board of education of Toronto in connection with an enlargement of their facilities for aeronautical engineering. As to any money being available under the legislation now before the committee for the purpose mentioned by my hon. friend, he will be aware from the previous discussion that the only amount made available by this legislation is for Manitoba. No portion of the money could therefore be made available for technical education in Ontario.

Technical Education

What will happen to-morrow when young men read that this committee has passed a bill for the purpose of spending some part of 810,000,000 appropriated under the Technical Education Extension Act? Most of them will think that members of parliament can distribute part of $10,000,000 for education, and many of them will want a slice of that for their own education. They will tell us, "You voted $10,000,000, I hope personally to take advantage of that." It is embarrassing for members of parliament to whom such requests are directed. In our province we write to a gentleman who is in charge of this scheme, and he always answers very nicely the letters of recommendation which are sent for anyone who seeks to take advantage of that act. But to my knowledge very few, at least from my constituencjq have derived any benefit from it.
Before going any further, I should like to know from the minister if this act applies only to the sons of those on relief, or if it applies to any young man who is willing to learn a trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: TECHNICAL EDUCATION
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext: Perhaps I have not made it sufficiently clear that the legislation now before the committee is not designed to carry out the objects of the youth training program. This is merely a continuation of the Technical Education Act of 1919 in order that one province, Manitoba, which has not taken up its full allotment, may be permitted to do so. The form of the bill is similar to the amending acts of 1929 and 1934. I agree with my hon. friend that it would be unfortunate if the impression went out from this house that we are dealing in this bill with an appropriation of $10,000,000. But I am sure that we may rely upon the press to put the position correctly. The whole purpose of this bill is to permit one province, Manitoba, to take up what portion of its original grant under the act of 1919 may still be claimed under the provisions of that statute.

maintopic: TECHNICAL EDUCATION
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext:
I understand that the
federal government has nothing at all to do with the distribution of that money? Grants

are made to the provinces, which decide to what individuals the money shall be awarded; is that the idea? Or does the dominion government give scholarships from that amount to private individuals?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) may be confusing this bill with the youth training program. As I explained earlier in this discussion, legislation dealing with the youth training program will be introduced later in this session. The present bill has one object only, which is to permit Manitoba to take up its remaining portion of the allotment under the legislation of 1919. Under that legislation the dominion government made certain grants available annually for the assistance of technical education in the provinces. The procedure was that an agreement was entered into between the dominion government and the provincial government respecting the expenditure of the federal grant. That agreement, of course, was bound by the terms of the statute, which stated that not more than twenty-five per cent of the annual grant payable to any province should be used for acquiring land or erecting or improving buildings or supplying furnishings or equipment. I suggest to my hon. friend that the other matters to which he has referred would properly, and most usefully be considered, when we have before us the measure dealing with the youth training program. .

the minister has already mentioned, and which will appear on Hansard, been paid to the provinces, or to individuals?

speechtext:
Would it not be
possible to extend this bill? It has been very satisfactory in its operation in connection with technical education in Toronto-I am speaking of Toronto particularly-and the minister has seen Doctor Butt of the department of education in respect to his request for money for aeronautical training. Since this scheme has worked so well, would it not be possible to have more money appropriated so that the department might be able to meet the request of the Toronto board of education to carry on this excellent work, especially in view of the times in which we live?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: TECHNICAL EDUCATION
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext:
I doubt whether on that
point I can add anything to what I have already said. There is no lack of appreciation of the importance of aeronautical engineering,

Technical Education
nor has there been any disposition on the part of the government not to do its part in supporting aviation. But as I have suggested, that is done through the Department of Transport and the Department of National Defence. Under the present measure it is not proposed to extend the Technical Education Act apart from the one purpose indicated, namely, to permit Manitoba to take up its full allocation under the legislation.

maintopic: TECHNICAL EDUCATION
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext:
I fully appreciate that
this bill could not be extended beyond the specific point with which it deals. But I do not think there should be any misunderstanding either in the house or in the country as to the Technical Education Act itself, that is, the act by which assistance was rendered to the provinces for the purpose of technical education. I feel quite sure that most of the allocation to British Columbia was spent in the city of Vancouver. I happened to have something to do with the school board there during part of the time when this money was being expended on technical schools and furnishings for those schools. But there is a great deal in the point that has been raised by a number of hon. members, particularly those from the city of Toronto, that the time is opportune for the passing of another technical education assistance act, because I doubt if the demand on the school boards of the various cities for technical education was ever as great as it is now, and I do not believe the youth training projects will meet that demand in its entirety. That again, I think, is something separate. I believe the time is opportune for the government to give consideration to the extension of aid of this kind to the educational authorities in the various provinces.

maintopic: TECHNICAL EDUCATION
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext:
I do not like to repeat what has been said already. The minister no doubt has seen this brief from the board of education of the city of Toronto, and I think he will realize that there is not sufficient space in the main building of the school in question. They went to the extent of renting a garage, or something like that, as a temporary arrangement, because the building is so badly crowded. I should like to point out the success they have had in their endeavour. One hundred boys have graduated from this four year course, and ninety per cent of those boys are employed at the present time, most of them, I understand, by firms engaged in aircraft production. Some have obtained positions with firms that put a premium on a high degree of efficiency,
accuracy and care. Thirty-six boys graduated from the aircraft course, of whom twenty-one have secured employment.
As I understand it, this act had the dual purpose of making grants for the education of the youth as well as providing accommodation for the education of these boys. When we think of the number of young boys walking around these days who have never had jobs, it seems to me that the government might take into consideration the further extension of this act, because it has worked very well so far. I believe, too, that these men who are giving of their time in the city of Toronto, the board of education, an excellent body which is doing such great work, should have their efforts appreciated and that they should be allowed to carry on this work. They are the people who have most to do with the education of these boys, and I believe it would be a splendid thing if these people had the money to spend on the necessary buildings and equipment. So I would ask the minister to consider extending this bill to serve further the purpose that it has served previously.

maintopic: TECHNICAL EDUCATION
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext:
Supplementing what I said a few moments ago in favour of consideration of the introduction of a further technical education act providing new and additional grants, I should like to leave a thought with the minister, which in turn he might present to his colleagues when dealing with the matter, in a light which probably has not occurred to him. We are all agreed that it would be a real contribution to the solution of the unemployment problem, particularly among the youth of the country, to provide further technical education in certain lines of mechanics. We are also aware that a terrific handicap is at present placed upon boards of education, certainly in urban centres, by the burden of municipal taxation. Within its jurisdiction this government probably cannot very well make a contribution towards the direct relief of that burden of taxation, because the municipalities are creatures of the province. I suggest to the minister, however, that this government might make a contribution to the relief of that burden in an indirect way. That is, they might further advance technical education, thus helping to solve the problem of unemployment among our youth, by making new grants for technical education which could be taken advantage of by the municipalities without imposing a further burden of municipal taxation upon property owners in the municipality.
If the government does not consider that a wise and feasible suggestion then might I suggest to the minister, in view of the fact
Technical Education

that Ontario has not cooperated in taking advantage of the money already granted for youth training projects, and in view of the fact that the minister has intimated that later in the session there will be introduced a youth training project which will be a three year plan, that before the introduction of that new legislation he might advantageously confer with the minister of labour of Ontario in an endeavour to 'bring down in this house a plan under which the government of that province will cooperate, so that Ontario youths may obtain the benefit of these training projects. In any event, if agreement cannot be reached, when that bill comes down in this house the minister will be able to advise us as to why it is not possible to get that measure of cooperation which we all so much desire.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: TECHNICAL EDUCATION
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext:
Dealing first with the
observations of the hon. member for St. Paul's, I agree entirely with him as to the value of the work done by the technical schools of the city of Toronto. As a matter of fact I was greatly impressed by what was presented to me by the delegation from the board of education of that city. On the other hand, I was obliged to tell them that there was no federal appropriation from which a grant could be made for the construction or enlargement of the technical school in which aeronautical engineering was being taught. I believe they went away persuaded that this was the case, though naturally they were disappointed and would have been pleased if they had received word that they could be given some direct financial assistance.
As to the point raised by the hon. member for York South, under the youth training program provision is not made for capital equipment. We do contribute to rentals of buildings and equipment, but our thought was that those who were enrolled for training should receive the maximum benefit of the various training projects. At the same time we felt that most of the provinces would be able, through their schools, to provide facilities for training purposes. We did not wish to duplicate those facilities, and in that I believe we were following a sound and economical course. .
As to Ontario not having taken up its full allocation under the youth training program, I can say only that in the present year, according to my present knowledge of the amount actually expended, there is still available for that province the sum of about $220,000.

maintopic: TECHNICAL EDUCATION
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext: That is more than I had thought. I believe I mentioned the sum of $135,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: TECHNICAL EDUCATION
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext: I shall ascertain the exact figure and see that it appears correctly in Hansard to-morrow. However, the full amount has not been taken up in Ontario, as it has in all the other provinces. It is, of course, for each province to determine what projects shall be established. Naturally any government in dealing with these matters is governed by consideration of what expenditures are most urgent. It is not a case of doing this and that, but rather a case of doing this or that. We did feel, and it is still my view, that the most urgent need comes from unemployed groups, and that is why through the youth training program we have been attempting to give special assistance to unemployed young people. Under a renewal of the Technical Education Act we would be assisting unemployed groups only in a limited degree-a much more limited degree than we are assisting them under the youth training program.

Other encouraging statistics are as to the number of younger men in the penitentiaries. The hon. member for Kootenay East thought the number of younger men in the penitentiaries had increased in an alarming way, but that is not so. I will give the number of young men under twenty-one, in the penitentiaries for a certain number of years. In 1929 the number was 322. That is a good deal too many but the number has not increased compared with later years. In 1930 the number of young men under twenty-one in the penitentiaries was 377; in 1931, 484; in 1932. 527; in 1933, 467; in 1934, 409; in
1935,	325; in 1936, 280; in 1937, 317. I am sorry I have not the figures for 1938, but the numbers in 1936 and 1937 were smaller than in 1929, in a period of great prosperity.
The number between the ages of twenty-one and thirty is perhaps a little larger. In 1937, there were 1,515 men between those ages in the penitentiaries, while in 1929 there were 1,270. On the other hand, in. 1932 the number was 1,900; in 1933, 2,052; in 1934, 1,916. So the number has been decreasing rather than increasing since 1933. The figures for men between the ages of thirty and forty are in about the same proportion. I suppose the committee is not interested in knowing the numbers between forty and fifty, and between fifty and sixty, because it was rather with regard to the younger men that questions were asked.
Those figures, Mr. Chairman, show the vastness of the problem, and I feel that those who thought a commission of three was unnecessary to administer such an important branch of the affairs of our country did not grasp the magnitude of the work to be done or the contact, supervision and control which the heads of the penitentiary branch must exercise over this considerable population of convicts and in the management of every one of these institutions. There is, of course, this other feature, the great importance of improving in every way possible not only

the management but ways and means of reforming those who are susceptible to reformation, and to give to that branch of social service in every way the consideration and attention which it deserves.

I would suggest to the
minister that in order to get a complete picture of the criminal problem, although perhaps this does not definitely relate to the bill under discussion, we should have statistics of the prison population in provincial institutions. maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had
expected the minister to tell us in a general way something about the improvements that are proposed. Not having received the bill until a few minutes ago, I have had no chance to look through it, and it is difficult to discuss the clauses unless we have some idea of what is proposed to be done. I understood the minister to say that we are going to have a commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: That is all.

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
I am opposed to any
more commissions unless they are of civil servants under the department. But if we are to have an independent commission with full power to do what it likes in the matter of employing people-and I see this commission has the right to select guards and all that-I never saw a commission yet that, in the spending of money, did not go away beyond the expectations of those who created it, and unless some limit is imposed upon the power of employing anyone and everyone it wishes to employ, I am not in accord with this commission idea.
Apart from that, I remember very well that when the minister was speaking on this question a year ago, something was said to the effect that other methods would be introduced to cure the evils that had apparently grown up in our penitentiary system. If the bill has in it anything in that regard I should like the minister to let us know. If it has, I shall have some further comments to make.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: I wonder whether my hon. friend was in the house when the resolution was being discussed.

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
Yes, I was.
TMr. E. Lapointe.]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
Well, I cannot say more than I said at that time. This bill, although it seems to be a voluminous document, is really a reenactment of the Penitentiary Act as it was, in all its provisions, except that a commission of three, instead of a superintendent, is to administer the penitentiaries.
As to the reforms to be made, some of them, as I said yesterday, are merely changes in the regulations which do not necessitate waiting for the appointment of the commission. But the recommendations of the investigating commissioners will be given effect by means of legislation. My purpose-and it was also one of the recommendations of the commissioners-is that such legislation should be scrutinized in the light of the conditions which the new commission will find, and approved, before it is submitted to parliament by the Minister of Justice, under whose control the penitentiaries branch will continue to be.
So I cannot give my hon. friend more details about the bill. He says that he is opposed to a commission because he does not know of any commission which has not spread and has not expanded its activities. My hope is that the penitentiaries commission will expand its activities in this momentous part of the civil service. There are reforms which have been suggested which may be commendable-the Borstal system, for instance, which is one way of attending to the young offenders; and there are other ways. But the Borstal or any other system cannot be put into operation without the proper buildings, without the accommodation necessary for that purpose, so that a pretty large expenditure is involved. As I said, this will have to be carefully studied and considered by the commission which will be at the head of this service and will, I hope, consist of men of ability and experience who will help myself, the government and parliament to do our duty in this regard.

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
I certainly hope that the objective the minister has in mind will be carried out. As was said the other evening

and there is no harm in repeating it-the house has confidence in the minister himself, and perhaps the system would have done better under his direction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend, but some people do not think so.

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
I have had some experience in investigating prison reform. I spent some time two years ago in investigating Wakefield, near Leeds, looking into the Borstal system.

Penitentiaries Commission

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: Which prison?

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
Near Leeds. Wakefield is about eight miles or less from Leeds.
I had the good fortune to meet, in the city itself, a gentleman who, I believe, was the original proposer of the idea that humane treatment of prisoners would work a marvellous reform, and be much more effective than ill treatment.

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
How long did the hon.
member serve there?

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
I will state that in a
few minutes. At Wakefield I learned that the official who had introduced the system there had been transferred to Barlinnie prison at Glasgow; in fact I got a telegram from the home office suggesting that I could proceed to Barlinnie and discuss the subject with the man who, more than any other I was told, was responsible for making the Borstal system a success. The minister will not mind if I tell him that I spent seven hours in Barlinnie, not of course as a prisoner. I wanted to understand thoroughly how the reform plan was being carried out. After reading the report through, what I have been wondering is if it is the intention of the department- I believe it is-to instruct the commissioners to carry out to the best advantage, of course under Canadian conditions, the means and methods which have resulted in such a reduction in the old country of second offenders, third offenders and so forth. Certainly they have had great results over there; compared with what I have observed here in Canada the results they have achieved are remarkable.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: Yes, but my hon. friend realizes our difficulties in Canada, because of the provincial gaols.

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: Yes, I was just coming to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: We cannot do what they are doing over there, because we have no control over a very large number of prisoners.

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
I was just coming to that matter, and further, to the fact that conditions of administration and taking care of offenders are much more difficult here than in the old land because over there, if an offender escapes, he cannot get off the island, and the effect is that the incentive to try to escape is not one-two-three in the old country what it is in Canada and the United States where escaped prisoners can go such long distances and move from one country to another.
In reference to what the minister has just said about the difficulty of administering prison affairs and reforms in Canada compared with England because of the amount of control retained by the provinces, on reading over the report I noticed that the second of the eighteen recommendations made by the commission is:
An immediate conference between the federal and provincial authorities should be held with a view to obtaining the full cooperation of the provincial authorities in putting the recommendations of the commission into effect.
I should like to know whether that conference has been held. It has not been held?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: No. As I stated last year when I tried to get the immediate appointment of that commission, I desire the commission to take over and study the whole problem before we communicate with the provinces.

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: The whole problem, as I said, is one of reducing the number of second and third offenders and so forth; in other words, of improving by proper administration the mentality and the inclination of the prisoner himself to really reform. I assume that is the main objective of the report. There is nothing I can add in view of what the minister has just said.

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: The minister has given the convict population of the eight penitentiaries in the nine provinces. I wonder if he would explain how the distribution of [DOT]those convicts is carried out. I do not think, for instance, to take the one in British Columbia, that the number 328 necessarily means that they are all prisoners convicted in British Columbia, does it? They are moved about from province to province in accordance with certain views of the superintendent. Will that distribution now be in the hands of the commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
Generally speaking, the population of the British Columbia penitentiary is composed of prisoners sentenced in that province. In Prince Albert they are the prisoners sentenced in Alberta and Saskatchewan; in Manitoba there is Stoney Mountain; in Ontario, Kingston; in Quebec, St. Vincent de Paul; and in the three maritime provinces, Dorchester. It happens occasionally that for the good of the management-and the minister has power in this regard-transfers are made from one penitentiary to another, but that is because of exceptional circumstances. For instance, as was said yesterday, a certain number of men were transferred a couple of weeks ago from
Penitentiaries Commission

Kingston to the western penitentiaries. That was because of overcrowding in Kingston. We hope that with the improvements which will be made and the necessary enlargement of the buildings in the various penitentiaries this will be avoided in the future, and there is actually in Kingston extension work being carried on which subsequently will provide the necessary space. These transfers are made with great care and there has been no trouble of any kind. The convicts have suffered no ill effects as a result, and as a matter of fact they are much better off in a prison in which there is adequate accommodation than they would be if they were crowded, as they were in Kingston, owing to an increase in population. Generally speaking, each penitentiary serves a certain section of the country.

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: The female convicts are all congregated at Kingston?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: They are all at Kingston, and I am pleased to say the number is very small. There are at present thirty-one female convicts in Canada, which speaks well for the weaker sex.

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: I have read quite closely the report of the royal commission and I must say I was much surprised at it. There seems to be, according to the report, hardly any penitentiary in Canada, which has been conducted properly in the past. The commissioners found fault with the guards, with those in charge, with the commissary, with the stewards in every penitentiary, with the recreation and schools. In fact, there was no branch of the penitentiary service that was not ' severely criticized in the report. What particular qualifications had these commissioners to pass such severe censure upon the penitentiaries of the country? Unfortunately we have had penitentiaries in Canada for a good many years; but surely the majority of the men in charge of these institutions must have been better qualified for the work they were doing than this commission has given them credit for. I consider the report a severe criticism of the administration of our Oanadian penitentiaries. Have any changes been already made in the administration of the penitentiaries, on the basis of the commission's report?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
As regards the first question, I may repeat what I said yesterday. The commission to investigate penitentiaries was appointed because of public demand which had been heard for many years and which had become increasingly difficult to resist, and more particularly because

of troubles in penitentiaries prior to the setting up of that commission. At one time there was considerable trouble in some of the penitentiaries, and the press of Canada had been insisting upon an investigation.
When it came to the appointment of the commissioners there was difficulty, just as the appointment of a permanent commission will be a difficult task to perform. The three commissioners first appointed were these: There was Mr. Justice Archambault, who is a judge of the high court of the province of Quebec, who had great experience in criminal matters, having been crown prosecutor for the district of Montreal, which I suppose was the largest in the country for many years. Then there was Mr. Anderson, then editor of the Globe. The press had taken such an interest in this matter that it was thought advisable to have from among its number a permanent member on the commission. Unfortunately my good friend Mr. Anderson died almost immediately after he was appointed. Mr. McRuer, K.C., who was appointed to replace him, was recommended more particularly by those who had been very much pleased with the appointment of Mr. Anderson-I refer to that section of the community which was impressed with the idea that some improvements ought to 'be made and some changes effected. The same element, more especially those who are interested in prison reform and who had recommended Mr. Anderson, were also recommending Mr. McRuer. Mr. McRuer had had a wide experience not only in legal matters but in criminal law, having been counsel on commissions concerned with some penitentiary troubles and other matters. As regards the other commissioner, we thought we should have a western man, and Mr. Craig, K.C., of Winnipeg, who was also crown counsel, having been attorney general of Manitoba for some years, was appointed. Of course it is always possible to criticize any appointment, but we try to get the best men possible. Others might prefer other names, but we thought we could not do better than appoint these three men. My hon. friend may not be satisfied with all they say in that report, but one thing he will admit, that the report evidences a great amount of work on the part of those commissioners.
As to the other question, I repeat what I said last year-and that is rvhy I was very sorry that the bill did not become law last year. I do not want those recommendations put into effect before this commission is appointed and before those men, who are expert and who devote their ability to this service, have an opportunity to consider carefully every one of those recommendations.

Penitentiaries Commission
Then I as Minister of Justice, on their report, will submit to parliament any legislation which is necessary.

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
I am concerned
about the long delay in getting something done along these lines. I notice the summary of recommendations of the commission contains some eighty-eight clauses. This is a pretty wide program, and while it is true that in making the recommendations the commissioners did urge that a commission should be appointed at once, they also recognized that there would have to be a well planned program. Two questions occur to me in this connection. A number of these recommendations deal with much more than the care of people in penitentiaries. The other night the minister said:
This legislation is to take care of prisoners. Of course the heads of penitentiaries are vitally interested in anything which would tend to cure existing evils and help reform the men committed to their charge, as well as to protect society against them.
Evidently this bill is intended primarily to take care of prisoners, but -what is to be done about the larger program of crime prevention? Is that to come specifically under the charge of these commissioners to be appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: The prevention of crime is as much my hon. friend's responsibility as my own; that is, the work of all men who are interested in social matters, not specifically the work of the management of penitentiaries.

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: But that is part of the work that must be undertaken, according to the report of the commissioners. We live in a scientific age, and I do not think most of us believe that people commit crimes because of native depravity. We recognize that there are certain conditions of environment which tend to foster crime. Some people may be bom better and some worse, but in practice I think people with decent environment have a much better chance to live a decent sort of life, and will do so; whereas if people have to live in slums, half starved and subject to temptation on all sides, they are more likely to go wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: I quite agree with my hon. friend.

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
I am very glad; I thought the minister would. My first question is: Who is going to be charged with this special task of trying to discover those causes which lead to crime, and setting to work in our communities those remedial agencies which at least help to prevent the production of
criminals? So far as I have been able to learn by glancing at the bill, there does not seem to me much in it that would provide for that. Are we to have nothing in the way of implementing that broader program?
Then there are a number of recommendations which seem to call for pretty definite legislation. I mentioned one the other night, that of the indeterminate sentence. There is a suggestion or recommendation of a somewhat extensive revision of the criminal code, and new classifications of prisoners. My second question is, these commissioners having been appointed-and I was delighted that the minister came out in such a forthright way and said there would be no political considerations in their appointment, but they would be men who would commend themselves to the public generally-I should like to know whether these new commissioners will have the machinery at their disposal so that they can carry out this program without waiting another year, thus delaying action long overdue.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
The prevention of crime of course is a matter in which we are all interested. My hon. friend suggested the abolition of slums, which are hotbeds of crime; he is quite right, but of course this will have to be dealt with in conjunction with other branches of the service and with the provinces. Here again there are certain spheres or domains on which we cannot very well trespass. But we all have the matter at heart, and I have no doubt that the men who will be at the head of this penitentiaries commission will do their best to cooperate with any other authority in any measures which would lead to the suppression of crime.
The treatment in prisons may have much to do with reforming men. There are two schools of thought in Canada as elsewhere; there is the one that thinks criminals are criminals anyway, that they are born so and that we should not try to reform them. I think that school is wrong. At the other extreme are those who would have them pampered, and released as soon as possible. But the protection of society must always be considered. Those two points of view have to be taken into account in dealing with this matter. For the benefit of the first school, those who say we should not do anything for the criminal, I point out that in a study made before that royal commission it is shown that on January 1, 1938, 188 prisoners confined in Canadian penitentiaries had been convicted more than ten times, and have cost the public of this country approximately $4,500,000, or $25,000 each. So, if we look
Penitentiaries Commission

at the question only from the point of view of cost in dollars and cents to the taxpayer, without any regard to the humanitarian aspect, the answer is still the same; society and the country are interested in trying to prevent this recidivism which costs the people of Canada so much, as well as making those men a danger to their fellow men, and derelicts without hope in this world.
That is where the question of the young offenders comes to the fore, and it ought to be taken care of and dealt with in the best possible way. There is no doubt that to send to the penitentiaries young men who may have made only one mistake, and to mix them up with hardened criminals, makes those young men lose what they had in the world in the way of opportunity and hope. It is our duty and the duty of all those who want to improve conditions in this country to try to bring about the best possible conditions not only in prison management but in the other, larger questions which my hon. friend has mentioned.

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
Then there is the
second question. Is the minister convinced that we have sufficient machinery, that is, are sufficient changes being made in the law, to permit these commissioners to go to work immediately? Can they make the classifications and do the other things that are recommended by the royal commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: Of course we have the whole branch, which is a pretty effective machine at the present time. The commission will have the present staff. The inspectors will become assistant commissioners; they will change their title, but they will be the same officers, and of course there will be need of additional officers if we carry out all the recommendations. But as the commission itself stated, the changes will have to be made gradually, by stages or instalments, if you like. That is the only way to achieve real and lasting progress.

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: For instance, there are changes that will have to be made in the criminal code. The commissioners would not have the right to alter the criminal code, yet the royal commission suggested that changes should be made at once.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
This all
goes together. I should like to make the changes in the criminal code in cooperation with the commission, when it is appointed.
