maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to appoint a commission with power under the minister to control, administer and manage the penitentiaries of the country. We have been criticized by our Tory friends for appointing a commission for this particular purpose. On former occasions there has been criticism of the government with respect to its not carrying out the recommendations of different commissions. The chief recommendation of the commission which investigated the penitentiaries and made a study of the penal system in Canada was to the effect that under our present system the problem of penal administration is too large in scope and too serious in results to be left in the hands of one man.

In his criticism yesterday, when, speaking on the resolution prior to the introduction of the bill, the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson) said the commission was being appointed for the purpose of shifting responsibility. To any one who has read the report of the commission on penal institutions it must be evident that one man was not capable, as superintendent of our institutions, to carry on the work. No country in the world lags as far behind in penology as does this Dominion of Canada. I am not a penologist, a criminologist or a sociologist, but I have read the report, and have made a study of it. I have made it my business to visit one of the largest penal institutions in Canada, and have spent some time therein viewing conditions and studying problems in the hope that when the bill came before the house I, looking at some of these problems from the point of view of the medical man, might be in a position to make to a commission some recommendations tending to bring about a betterment of conditions in our institutions.
It is remarkable that the public has always shown an absorbing interest in criminals. Newspapers devote much of their space to the subject, even to the prejudice of law enforcement bodies, to such an extent that J. Edgar Hoover, chief of the United States federal bureau of investigation, has protested again and again that the publicity given criminals encourages crime. The tendency of recent years, expressed in tabloids and in the moving pictures, has been to give the hero role to the police rather than to the criminal, and the shift is said to be obtaining results. But whether the neighbourhood boys play G-man, mounted police or gunman, adult interest is still centred in the criminal, as it has been from Homer to Dickens, Zola and Hugo. This interest has, of more recent years, sold thousands of crime and detective stories, and has proved a gold-mine to publishers and authors of such works.
A noted criminologist, J. L. Gillin, attributes this phenomenon to public interest in human conduct, which is greater in proportion to the unusualness of such conduct. In so far as most citizens lead lives which do not violate the standards approved by society, the unusual person stands out the more clearly. Psychologists explain also that until fairly modern times man has been constantly subjected to danger, and that danger has two reactions: cowardice and courage. Danger still provides a thrill to be met with appropriate activity, and in following the careers of criminals, the honest citizen vicariously experiences this thrill without the accompanying activity and danger. LTnfortunatefy this interest does not

Penitentiaries Commission
extend beyond the apprehension, trial and conviction of the criminal. Just as books of romance end with wedding bells, books of crime usually end with the clanging of prison gates.
So much for the general public interest in crime and criminals. There is, however, another and more serious approach to the subject -interest in crime and criminals as a social phenomenon-a social disease to be met and, in so far as is possible, eradicated by scientific study and scientific treatment. This scientific study, which includes the process of making laws, breaking laws, and reacting toward the breaking of laws, is directed to the end of protecting society. Any scientific study of criminology must have this objective constantly in mind, whether it is to be attained by prevention of crime, apprehension of the criminal, punishment or reform.
We should keep in mind, Mr. Chairman, that the main purpose of any penal system is, first, to protect society, and, second, the regeneration, education and rehabilitation of criminals.
It may be redundant to quote the axiom that "prevention is better than cure," but in our methods of crime control this precept is far from being adequately observed. We are too prone to stint expenditures at the outset in preventive work through schools, boys' clubs, and juvenile courts, and to spend large sums in the apprehension and imprisonment of adult criminals when cure is all but hopeless. At the same time we regard soaring costs of crime with dismay.
It has been estimated that the total cost of criminal justice in the United States costs that country in excess of three hundred and fifty million dollars a year, and estimates of the total cost of crime have run as high as thirteen billions. While these figures, particularly the latter, are far from accurate, they give some indication of the enormous expense which is thrown upon the general public by criminal activities. In the report of the royal commission to investigate the penal system of Canada, it is estimated that the cost of 188 recidivists in Canadian penitentiaries at the date of the investigation had cost Canadian taxpayers over four and a half million dollars, or $25,000 a man. That is a figure which was also given by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) when he was speaking. These figures show us that money spent in the prevention of crime would be money well spent. If, by the provision of, say $1,000 in juvenile crime prevention, we can prevent a juvenile from becoming a hardened recidivist, who will cost the taxpayer over $25,000 before his useless life is ended, we shall be saving $24,000 rather than spending $1,000.
Crime prevention begins in the home and may be attacked from the general angle of correcting undesirable social conditions-the clearing of slums, better housing, a higher standard of living, health control, employment opportunities, and adult education-or from the particular angle of family or domestic relations courts, boys' club activities, and the school.
Students of criminology assign the main social condition causing crime to deficiencies in the home life of the child, manifested by poor training, lack of discipline and emotional instability. This may occur in the homes of the rich, where the parents have other interests and leave their children to the care of servants or to their own devices, or in the homes of the poor, where adverse economic conditions press upon family life. But when heredity influences are also present, and the parents are emotionally unstable and temperamentally maladjusted, the child, in addition to lack of proper discipline and care, will inherit the disordered emotional system of his parents, requiring the best, rather than the worst, of care to correct. Broken homes, where there is divorce, disharmony or a step-parent, or where the child is reared by disinterested relatives, will also provide a favourable breeding place for juvenile delinquency.
The preventive approach to such problems is through the family court, where broken homes come to the attention of the authorities. Let me mention here that perhaps no city in the whole of Canada is more to be commended than Ottawa for the introduction and the carrying on of the family court which investigates the conditions which underlie crime in this city.
The preventive approach, as I was saying, is through the family court; second, through the school, where emotional, physical or mental deficiencies may be detected, and. third, through boys' clubs where lack of parental training and discipline will become apparent. When, through any of these agencies, character deficiencies or undesirable environmental influences of the juvenile are detected, immediate action should be taken through social agencies to' correct the dangerous trends that have been discovered. It is here that society should spend without stint some portion of those many millions that will later have to be spent if preventive measures fail.
There will always be cases in which dangerous trends are not discovered in time or where preventive measures will fail. There will also be those cases where no criminal or anti-social attitude is present but where
155S
Penitentiaries Commission

emotional strains will prove too much for the emotional control of the individual, and manslaughter or murder will result. There will also be cases where temptation exceeds powers of resistance, and embezzlement or other form of theft will be committed. For these cases special adult treatment will have to be provided.
The question of this adult treatment is one which is engaging the best thought of penologists in every civilized country, and no general panacea has as yet been evolved. Human behaviour being individualistic, it is improbable that any - general theory will ever be entirely successful.
Canada, as the report of the royal commission has demonstrated, is lagging behind in penological matters, and the bill before us at this time is the first step in a program to bring this country abreast of the times.
The lag in our development is not an unmixed evil, because it gives us an opportunity to study the methods of those countries which have outdistanced us and to select from their systems the best features already proved to be successful, as well as to profit by their mistakes.
That development in modern penological treatment which has met with the most outstanding success has been classification, segregation, and the special treatment of special types of prisoners. Such classification depends upon the buildings available and the distances to be overcome, but in so far as these considerations have permitted, classification has been the most successful treatment which has been yet evolved.
The types which require to be classified and segregated are: First, the insane; second, the subnormal; third, drug addicts; fourth, young offenders; fifth, hardened recidivists; sixth, first offenders and accidental criminals. The remainder of the criminal population will form a final class which will be the largest of all.
The treatment of insane persons and drug addicts is one for specialized medical attention.
With reference to subnormals, those who cannot be certified as definitely insane within the meaning of the Penitentiary Act, but who have obvious deficiencies, should not be permitted to mingle with the general prison population, because they cannot appreciate the necessity of observing prison discipline and because they are victimized by the more intelligent and troublesome prisoners who may aggravate their mental condition or urge them into rebellion and revolt in which the

instigators do not participate. That, Mr. Chairman, I submit, is one of the principal reasons why we have had in Canadian penitentiaries throughout the last number of years a great number of riots and insurrections.
Hardened recidivists should be subjected to preventive detention. It is known that their period of freedom on release will be limited to a vacation and that they will surely revert to crime, which is the only occupation they know or will follow, and will surely return to prison. These men are like lepers. They are unfit to live in society, and should therefore be segregated from it, not as a form of punishment but as the least expensive and most effective form of treatment. Their routine should not be onerous. They should have proper exercise, proper food and clothing, and some recreation, but they should not again be released to prey upon society.
I might remark here that I think well of the regulation in the United States whereby a criminal who has a number of convictions against him is finally sent to prison for life.
This applies also to the so-called sex criminal, who should be subjected to curative or corrective treatment and should never be permitted to advance along the well beaten and easily predictable path from indecency to murder. Let me say here that the vast percentage of indecency cases in the penal institutions of this country are cases of crimes which have been committed by men over fifty years of age. To the medical men that cannot point to anything but some type of physical disability which may be cured by modern surgical methods.
With regard to the accidental offender who has been overcome 'by a temptation too strong for him, or by the stress of an overmastering emotion, his sentence can be justified only by its deterrent effect upon others. This man is inclined to look upon his imprisonment as just retribution for his crime or as a penitence to be performed. There is no need of imprisonment or training for him; its only effect can be to deter others. He has learned his lesson before his sentence has commenced, and he is less likely to repeat a criminal offence than another is to commit one. His penal treatment should be so designed as to keep him from becoming bitter, while preparing him for a resumption of his normal life. With regard to this type of offender it can be truly said, " There, but for the grace of God, go I"; for who knows what he may do under pressure of circumstances when confronted by some immediate and compelling emotional crisis.

Penitentiaries Commission
With regard to young offenders, special individual treatment must be given. These youths are still in their formative years. Wrong ideals can still be corrected. The influence of early environment and associations can be eradicated. New and worthwhile objectives can still be made attractive. But the task is a difficult one, and failure will but confirm the youth in his anti-social point of view.
One of the things which struck me on my visit to the Kingston penitentiary was the great number of young men who were in that institution. I happened to be there about the time they were coming in for their noonday meal; and one would think, from the appearance of the men who were entering in file at that particular time, that one was looking upon the campus of Queen's university rather than a penitentiary. I was told by the warden of Kingston penitentiary that the average age of those within that institution is twenty-four years; and the day I was there there were 783 prisoners. It is a sad reflection on our present sociological system, when so many young men coming from broken homes have to start off their career in the penitentiaries.
Youths at this age revolt against the humdrum routine and irksome responsibilities with which the world confronts them. They crave adventure, romance, admiration, and the immediate realization of their dreams. They are thoughtless, reckless, animalistic, not yet socialized. It is not surprising that the slow and plodding road of honest endeavour should repel them, and that lawlessness, with its apparent quick result, should attract them. They must have their heroes, and if these heroes are big-shot gangsters they will take pride in being tough and hard, and will be sullenly resistant to any attempt to influence them. It is necessary to substitute a more desirable hero, and the man who can do so must possess their confidence and something of their admiration before he can succeed. That is why the Borstal system, which is dependent upon the Borstal staff, has shown such satisfactory results. To deal with this type of offender we must develop a type of prison officer that is individually exceptional.
I ask you, Mr. Chairman, what makes young men in this country want to join the mounted police? Because it offers them a career. There is a glamour, something about it which appeals to them. When this prison commission is set up, one of the first things it should do is attempt to have guards of a higher quality and of a higher classification than the present guards at our institutions. I would suggest
that our universities give a special course to young men who would take up this particular career. After training along the lines of penology to a limited extent with a high type of man has been given, you will have the men in the prisons look up to these men who are their guards and their trainers, and they will have beneficial effects on the men who are confined. That is exactly why the Borstal system has been the success which it has.
I have heard it said on several occasions that the Borstal system should be introduced into this country. I do not think it is any better system than we have in Ontario in what is known as the parole system. That system could be adapted to advantage to the whole of Canada; instead of introducing a new system we could have a further extension of the parole system which we have for the penal institutions of Ontario.

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: The Borstal system operates in the prison or in properties adjacent to the prison.

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
My contention is that the parole system is as good as the Borstal system, although I readily understand that the two have separate functions.
With regard to the large remaining class, the ordinary second or third offender, who is neither mentally deficient nor addicted to drugs, who is neither a first offender nor a hardened recidivist, we must give them moral hospitalization and treatment. In this we can look to the medical profession for guidance.
What would we think of a physician who, diagnosing typhoid fever, said to his patient, "I am sending you to the hospital because you have typhoid fever. You will remain there for two weeks. During that time, food, shelter and a bed will be provided, but no treatment will be given for the disease. At the end of two weeks you will be discharged whether you have recovered before that time, at that time, or not yet." We would regard such a physician as a madman; yet we do exactly that with our morally sick. It is long past the time for us to change this procedure. We must diagnose the criminal's condition and prescribe his treatment. From what contaminated source did this condition arise? What incubated it? Only by understanding the particular case can we prescribe the proper treatment. How long should the man be hospitalized? Obviously, until he is cured. Some conditions can be cured immediately; some require time; some may be incurable, and a man is fit to be discharged only when he is cured. At that time hospitalization
Penitentiaries Commission

should cease and convalescence should commence. If the man has a relapse it does not mean that we should be discouraged. We must resume the cure and make more certain that next time it is effective.
During convalescence we cannot expect the man to compete on an equal footing with people in robust health. He must still be under the supervision of his physician, who can give him necessary treatment, and who can watch for indications of a relapse.
We have passed the age when torture and beatings were prescribed for the cure of the insane. We no longer permit those with contagious diseases to mingle with surgical or other medical cases. We must progress with those who are morally ill as we have already progressed with those who are mentally or physically ill.
In this progression our greatest obstacle, as was the case in psychiatry and medicine, will be public indifference and public ignorance. If we give offenders in our penitentiaries special treatment and training we shall be accused of pampering the criminal. If we give him assistance and supervision after release, we shall be accused of discriminating against the honest man who is suffering economic hardship. We shall be asked why we assist ex-convicts to obtain employment when honest men are without jobs. We might as well be asked why a sick man, recently risen from a sick-bed. should require convalescence and treatments. The answer is the same in both cases: The treatment is to overcome a handicap and to place the man in a position to compete with those who are fit-not on a preferred basis, but on as nearly an equal basis as we can achieve. To do otherwise-thus ignoring the handicap of the discharged convict-is, whether his sentence be for thirty days or thirty years, to condemn him for life.
We must make up our minds to one of two courses: that dictated by reason and founded upon our experience in medicine and psychiatrj' and in most advanced and successful penal systems, which is the scientific curative method; or that dictated by ignorance and prejudice, which is barbarous and destructive. If the people of this country, misled by embittered cynicism or by indifferent stupidity, choose the latter course, they must be prepared to abide by the inevitable result -/nounting law-enforcement costs and increased viciousness in crime.
I think that we might at this time say a word or two with reference to some other matters with which the commission will have to deal. Let me say something first with regard [Mr. McCann.1
to the personnel of the commission. It cannot be a personnel of supermen. There are no such things as supermen; supermen exist as such only in their own minds. What we do want is a commission of men who have the humanitarian point of view. Our penal system has been run for years by men who have had entirely the militaristic point of view. We want men of education, learning, culture and some experience, but especially men who see the human side of things. It has been said that there should be a medical man on the commission. I do not agree with that suggestion. The commission should receive the advice of medical men; every man who is sent to a penal institution should be given the advantage of a proper physical examination, and his case should be studied individually with a view to seeing whether or not he has physical disabilities, the removal of which will improve his moral condition.
In visiting the institution at Kingston I find that the facilities, there for medical work are altogether inadequate. We have a makeshift hospital. I do not want to be too critical of the past administration or of the institution; but if we are to get anywhere in the treatment of those in our penal institutions, then we must improve the physical conditions under which they live. For instance, the whole outfit of buildings at Kingston is antiquated. The warden of that institution, showing me around, pointed with pride to the date-stone of one building, which said "1830." The remark which I might have made on that occasion but did not like to make was, "Your system is just as antiquated as are your buildings." They undertake to teach these prisoners a trade, but they have nothing like proper workshops. Their whole commissary department is antiquated. One gets the odour of it as soon as one enters the institution. All these things added together will make a criminal, even when he is within the prison, highly incorrigible, and embitter him against society, and it is to my mind one of the causes of many of the riots that we have had.
Another department which ought to undergo revamping is the remissions branch. Under the present system the remissions officer makes a recommendation to the minister with regard to any remissions of cases that are brought to his attention. In my opinion, instead of a remissions officer and remissions branch, the commission with their inspectors should constitute a parole board, and prisoners should be given an opportunity to appear before that board to present their particular case. I am sure there is not a member of this house, and very few clergymen in the country, who have not. been requested by friends of those who

Penitentiaries Commission
are in these institutions to use their influence with the remissions oflicer or with the Minister of Justice with a view to obtaining some remission of sentences imposed.
I have said something with reference to training. The present guards, as they are called, who are the officers in. charge of the prisoners, are taken from here, there and everywhere. They should be men especially adapted to that particular kind of work, and given some training for it. Schools should be established for the training of these people. Let me say in passing that in the city of Kingston there is another institution which houses almost twice as many inmates as are in the Kingston penitentiary, that is the Ontario Institute for the Insane. In my experience of twenty-five or thirty years observation. of that institution I have never heard of any insurrections or riots or irregularities, and I attribute that to the fact that the inmates are supervised by people who are trained for that supervision. There could not be a better exemplification of what in the one instance, trained officials can do, and what takes place when officials are without training.
Then, in connection with all these institutions, not enough consideration is given to what shall become of a man after he is discharged. Efforts should be put forth to rehabilitate him, restore him to society and make him a useful citizen. I suggest that the commission should give serious consideration to the appointment of a trained rehabilitation officer in every prison, who will give consideration to the individual cases, and months before the discharge of a prisoner will seek ways and means whereby that man will be rehabilitated and restored to the community.
However, I believe that the greatest progress that will be made in penology in this country in the next twenty-five years will be along medical and surgical lines; giving men a complete and thorough examination, seeking to classify them on the advice of trained psychiatrists and to remove the physical defects which so many have that aggravate their mental condition and make them go morally wrong. If a commission is to be set up in this country just for the purpose of having something new and transferring the work from the superintendent, without the Minister of Justice and his department having in the background a fixed determination to improve the condition of our penal institutions and the people in them, we might just as well not bother enacting this bill.

was removed merely because of a change of government certainly would have a claim against the government. The words " for cause " mean something which makes him unfit for office, not merely political opinions or things of that kind. Those words appear in most of the legislation appointing boards, and it has never been considered that there was danger in inserting that provision. I think they are rather a protection. Otherwise the government would be forced to keep in office for ten years a man who, for instance, might be unable to fulfil his task for physical or other reasons. I believe this is a protection for the country.

speechtext: Would the minister explain the procedure to be followed in making appointments? It seems clear that this bill does not provide for open, competitive examinations under the civil service commission. If this penitentiaries commission is to be established to correct the conditions which were disclosed by the report of the royal commission, I see no reason why it would not stabilize the service and remove influences tending to corruption if all appointments were placed under the civil service commission. maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
The
appointment of these officers was under the civil sendee commission while I was Minister of Justice previously, prior to 1930. In 1933 the then Minister of Justice introduced a bill placing the appointment of these officials under the governor general in council. I was on the opposition side at the time, but I must say that I gave the new legislation my full support. I have myself experienced the troubles caused by the former system. I cannot understand why the civil service com^ mission should have the responsibility of appointing wardens and deputy wardens, men who have convicts under their supervision, men who have most delicate work to do and carry tremendous responsibility. In the end the Minister of Justice is the one responsible for what happens in the penitentiaries. But there are troubles, and when those troubles develop they are of an extremely serious nature. There have been riots, rebellions and all sorts of disturbances. How can the civil service commission, rather than the one who in the end will bear the responsibility, appoint those who will be at the head of those institutions? The present system is working well. I assure my hon. friend that so far as I am concerned-and any Minister of Justice would do the same-I have to take the greatest possible care, because of the
Penitentiaries Commission

serious consequences. I know that in connection with that special work I have more confidence in myself than in the civil service commission.

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES

speechtext: I find myself in accord with the hon. member for Vancouver North. It must be realized that the Warden and deputy warden are the men primarily responsible for the discipline in their particular institutions. It seems to me that the bill is very weak in this section.

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL

maintopic: PENITENTIARIES

If my
